fields.title: Decisions That Shape Economics
fields.keyTakeaway: Margin is determined by freshness requirements, isolation model, share of background work, and dependence on external services with unit pricing—and the latter is most dangerous at scale.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Two competing products with the same price. Why does one have a 70% margin and the other 40%?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The difference in margin is determined by decisions made early on, when volumes are small and costs are imperceptible. Changing them later is expensive. A PM participating in these decisions impacts product economics more than through pricing.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Five architectural choices with the greatest impact on margin.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Data freshness requirement.** Real-time is multiple times more expensive than an hour delay: persistent connections, webhooks, recalculation per event instead of a schedule. Often a product requirement and unjustified.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Client isolation level.** Shared schema vs database per tenant from `DS3-N3`—maintenance cost difference is multiples. Determines which segment is profitable.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Share of work per user vs background.** Calculating on every request or once an hour for everyone. The second is dozens of times cheaper with the same result for the user.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Dependence on external services with unit pricing.** Acquiring, SMS, geocoding, models. Do not decrease with scale and become the dominant item during growth.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Stored volume and retention period.** Grows like an integral, and without an explicit decision, grows forever.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Common trait: **decisions that make cost proportional to user activity rather than the number of users are the most dangerous.** A product where an active user is 50x more expensive than an inactive one handles growth poorly—meaning it is penalized for success.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Economic breakdown across these five items.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Freshness.* Prices—hour, stock—real time. The second is expensive, but mandatory: discrepancy is visible to the user. Live price from the `PF2-G-B` gate is an example of an unjustified requirement.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Isolation.* Shared schema for 860 partners, separate for large ones on a corporate tier—the tier covers the difference.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Background work.* Recommendations recalculated every 6 hours rather than on request. Calculated difference—about 340k a month.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: *External services.* 23% of costs, with threefold growth will become 38%. The main economic risk.
fields.sections/3/blocks/6/text: Strategic conclusion: **further margin improvement lies in negotiations with acquiring and in reducing SMS, not in infrastructure.** The infrastructure part is already small relative to external services.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Economic optimization at an early stage is premature: while the product is searching for product-market fit, maintenance cost is not the main thing. The moment is when volumes become noticeable and growth is predictable.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Margin is determined by freshness requirements, isolation model, share of background work, and dependence on external services with unit pricing—and the latter is most dangerous at scale.
